SCOPING / ENDOSCOPY__Upper GI:
Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD, or gastroscopy) is a flexible endoscopic examination of the upper gastrointestinal tract — the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum — performed via the mouth. It is the first-line investigation for most upper GI symptoms, allows targeted biopsy (e.g. for H. pylori and coeliac disease), and doubles as a therapeutic tool for controlling bleeding, banding varices, dilating strictures and placing feeding tubes.

1Indications — diagnostic & therapeutic

Diagnostic OGD is driven by symptoms and red-flag (ALARM) features; therapeutic OGD is used to intervene directly on bleeding, varices and strictures.

🔬Dyspepsia + ALARMS55
Anaemia, Loss of weight, Anorexia, Recent-onset progressive symptoms, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty, age >55 — 2-week-wait referral
🩸Upper GI bleed
Haematemesis / melaena — diagnostic and therapeutic (within 24h, or immediately after resuscitation if unstable)
🍽️Dysphagia
Any new swallowing difficulty warrants urgent OGD to exclude oesophageal malignancy
🧬Coeliac / IDA
Duodenal (D2) biopsies for villous atrophy; investigation of unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia
🔁Barrett's surveillance
Periodic monitoring of metaplasia for dysplasia / early adenocarcinoma
🛠️Therapeutic
Variceal banding, ulcer haemostasis, stricture dilatation, PEG placement, polypectomy, foreign-body removal
New dysphagia or dyspepsia with ALARM features→Urgent 2-week-wait OGD to exclude upper GI cancer
Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia→OGD (+ colonoscopy) with duodenal biopsy to exclude coeliac and malignancy
2How it is performed

An outpatient day-case procedure using a flexible video endoscope passed under direct vision.

Fasting: nil by mouth for ≥6 hours (clear fluids often allowed up to 2h) to ensure an empty stomach and reduce aspiration risk.
Analgesia/sedation: local anaesthetic throat spray (lidocaine) to the pharynx, with or without IV conscious sedation (midazolam) ± opioid; a mouthguard protects the scope and teeth.
Position: left lateral decubitus, with continuous monitoring of oxygen saturations, and supplemental oxygen given.
Technique: the scope is advanced through the oropharynx, oesophagus, stomach and into the second part of the duodenum; air insufflation distends the lumen and the stomach is retroflexed to view the fundus and cardia.
Sampling: biopsies are taken for histology; antral biopsies for the CLO / rapid urease test detect H. pylori, and D2 biopsies assess for coeliac villous atrophy.
📷 Image placeholder — endoscopic view of the gastro-oesophageal junction showing salmon-pink Barrett's mucosa extending above the gastric folds.
3Key findings & interventions through the scope
🕳️Peptic ulcer
Gastric or duodenal ulcer; risk stratified by Forrest classification for rebleeding
🔥Oesophagitis
Reflux mucosal breaks graded by the Los Angeles (LA) classification A–D
🪱Varices
Oesophageal/gastric varices of portal hypertension — treated by band ligation
🍣Barrett's
Salmon-coloured columnar metaplasia at the GOJ — premalignant, needs biopsy/surveillance
🎗️Malignancy
Ulcerating or fungating mass / stricture — biopsy for diagnosis and staging
💢Mallory-Weiss tear
Linear mucosal tear at the GOJ after retching/vomiting — usually self-limiting
Actively bleeding / visible-vessel ulcer→Dual endoscopic therapy: adrenaline injection PLUS a second modality (clip or thermal) + high-dose PPI
Bleeding oesophageal varices→Endoscopic band ligation + terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics
Benign peptic stricture / achalasia→Balloon or bougie dilatation through the scope
4Complications, consent & pre-procedure checks
Perforation: the most serious complication — rare in diagnostic OGD but higher with dilatation or stenting; presents with pain, surgical emphysema and sepsis.
Bleeding: especially after biopsy, polypectomy or therapeutic intervention.
Aspiration: gastric contents into the airway, greater with sedation, active bleeding or a non-fasted stomach.
Sedation-related: respiratory depression and hypotension from midazolam — have flumazenil, oxygen and reversal to hand.
Minor: sore throat, bloating and transient discomfort are common and self-limiting.
Pre-procedure preparation→Informed consent, ≥6h fasting, IV access, and check/hold anticoagulants & antiplatelets for therapeutic (high-bleeding-risk) procedures
🚩 PERFORATION and ASPIRATION are the feared complications. Suspect perforation with post-procedure chest/abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia or surgical emphysema — confirm with contrast study/CT and involve surgery early. Adequate fasting and airway vigilance during sedation minimise aspiration; watch for sedation-induced respiratory depression and hypotension.
🎓 In upper GI bleeding, calculate a Glasgow-Blatchford score at presentation to guide admission (a score of 0 may allow outpatient management), then use the Rockall score after endoscopy for rebleeding/mortality risk. Bleeding ulcers should receive dual endoscopic therapy plus high-dose IV PPI.

Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) combines a flexible endoscope with a high-frequency ULTRASOUND probe mounted at its tip. Passed into the GI lumen much like an OGD, it sits the transducer millimetres from the target, giving exquisitely detailed cross-sectional imaging of the individual GI wall layers and the structures immediately adjacent — pancreas, biliary tree, mediastinum and regional lymph nodes. Its proximity to the target gives resolution of the wall layers and small lesions/nodes that far exceeds CT, and a linear echoendoscope lets the operator perform real-time EUS-guided FNA/FNB and therapeutic drainage.

1Indications — staging, characterising & sampling

EUS is primarily a locoregional STAGING and tissue-sampling tool, with a growing therapeutic role.

🔬Cancer staging
Locoregional T- and N-staging of oesophageal, gastric, rectal & pancreatic cancer
🔬Subepithelial lesions
Characterise submucosal masses — GIST, leiomyoma, cyst — by layer of origin
🔬Pancreatobiliary
Assess pancreatic mass, cystic lesions, chronic pancreatitis & biliary strictures
🔬EUS-FNA / FNB
Sample pancreatic masses & mediastinal / peri-GI lymph nodes for cytology/histology
Oesophageal / rectal cancer for curative treatment→EUS defines depth of wall invasion (T) & nodal involvement (N) to guide neoadjuvant vs surgery
Indeterminate pancreatic mass on CT→EUS-FNA/FNB for a tissue diagnosis before oncological treatment

Therapeutic uses (linear scope): EUS-guided drainage of pancreatic pseudocysts and walled-off necrosis, and coeliac plexus block/neurolysis for intractable pancreatic cancer pain.

2How it is performed
Preparation and route mirror OGD (upper GI) or flexible sigmoidoscopy (rectal): fasting, consent, IV access and conscious sedation ± throat spray, left-lateral position.
A radial echoendoscope gives 360° cross-sectional images ideal for staging/orientation; a linear echoendoscope images in the plane of the scope, allowing a needle to be watched in real time for FNA/FNB and drainage.
A water-filled balloon or instilled water improves acoustic coupling to the wall; Doppler identifies intervening vessels before any needle pass.
The normal GI wall is resolved into five alternating layers, letting the operator judge exactly how deep a tumour penetrates.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the endoscopic ultrasound view of the five-layer GI wall with an FNA needle sampling an adjacent node.
3Key findings & interventions
Tumour disrupting deeper wall layers→Higher T-stage — invasion through mucosa/submucosa into muscularis propria or beyond
Round, hypoechoic, well-demarcated node ≥10 mm→Suspicious for malignant node — target for FNA to confirm N-stage
Hypoechoic mass arising from 4th (muscularis propria) layer→Typical of GIST — sample and refer for resection/surveillance by size
Superior resolution of wall layers and small (<1 cm) lesions/nodes compared with CT, allowing accurate early T-staging.
Real-time FNA/FNB yields cytology or core histology from masses and nodes; therapeutic passes create a cystgastrostomy for pseudocyst/walled-off necrosis drainage.
4Complications & safety
Consent for a diagnostic ± therapeutic/sampling procedure, covering the specific FNA risks.
Fasting (typically 6 h food, 2 h clear fluids) to protect the airway during sedation.
Coagulation: check clotting/platelets and manage anticoagulants/antiplatelets before FNA, as needle passes carry a bleeding risk.
Shares OGD complications — perforation, bleeding, infection, and sedation-related aspiration/cardiorespiratory events.
🚩 EUS-FNA/FNB of a PANCREATIC lesion can precipitate acute PANCREATITIS; perforation and bleeding are the other feared complications — safeguard with clotting checks, Doppler vessel-avoidance and appropriate consent.
🎓 EUS is the most accurate modality for locoregional T-staging of GI cancers because the transducer sits directly against the wall — but it is operator-dependent and, unlike CT/PET, does NOT assess distant metastases, so it complements rather than replaces cross-sectional imaging.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) uses a side-viewing duodenoscope passed through the mouth to the second part of the duodenum, where the ampulla of Vater is cannulated, contrast injected and the biliary and pancreatic ducts imaged under fluoroscopy. Once a purely diagnostic test, it is now predominantly therapeutic — MRCP has replaced it for pure imaging — and is the workhorse for relieving biliary obstruction from stones, strictures and cholangitis.

1INDICATIONS — now mainly therapeutic

ERCP is reserved for cases where an intervention is planned. Diagnosis is otherwise done non-invasively with MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound.

🪨CBD stones
Choledocholithiasis — sphincterotomy + balloon/basket extraction
⛔Biliary stricture
Malignant (pancreatic/cholangiocarcinoma) or benign — stenting
🔥Cholangitis
Ascending infection — urgent biliary drainage/decompression
💧Bile leak
Post-cholecystectomy / trauma — stent to divert bile
🧪Pancreatic duct
Strictures, leaks, stones — pancreatic stenting/intervention
🩸Tissue sampling
Brushings/biopsy of indeterminate strictures for cytology
CBD stone on MRCP→Sphincterotomy + basket/balloon extraction
Malignant hilar/distal stricture→Plastic stent or self-expanding metal stent (SEMS)
Charcot triad + obstruction→Urgent ERCP drainage after resuscitation + antibiotics
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Position & anaesthesia: patient prone or semi-prone on the fluoroscopy table, under conscious sedation (midazolam + opioid) or general anaesthesia.
Intubation: the side-viewing duodenoscope is passed to the second part of the duodenum, bringing the ampulla of Vater into view.
Cannulation: the papilla is cannulated with a catheter/sphincterotome and guidewire; contrast is injected and the ducts imaged under fluoroscopy.
Sphincterotomy: the sphincter of Oddi is incised with a diathermy wire to widen the biliary orifice for access.
Clearance/therapy: a balloon or Dormia basket trawls the duct for stones; strictures are dilated and stented (plastic or metal).
📷 Image placeholder — endoscopic view of the ampulla of Vater with sphincterotome cannulating, plus fluoroscopic cholangiogram showing a filling defect (stone) in the common bile duct.
3FINDINGS & THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTIONS

The cholangiogram/pancreatogram is read for filling defects, strictures, dilatation and leaks; therapy follows in the same sitting.

Filling defect in CBD→Stone — extract with balloon/basket after sphincterotomy
Smooth vs shouldered stricture→Benign vs malignant — brush cytology + stent
Contrast extravasation→Bile leak — place stent to decompress and divert
Dilated duct proximal to block→Obstruction confirmed — drain with stent
4COMPLICATIONS & PRE-PROCEDURE SAFETY

ERCP is the most complication-prone routine endoscopic procedure; complications must be consented for explicitly.

🧪Post-ERCP pancreatitis
Commonest & most important — rectal NSAID prophylaxis ± PD stent
🩸Bleeding
Post-sphincterotomy haemorrhage — check coagulation first
🕳️Perforation
Duodenal or retroperitoneal — may need surgery
🦠Cholangitis/sepsis
Introduced infection above an incompletely drained obstruction
💊Sedation/contrast
Cardiorespiratory depression, aspiration, contrast reaction
Consent: explicitly mention post-ERCP pancreatitis, bleeding, perforation and infection risk.
Coagulation: check FBC/clotting; manage anticoagulants/antiplatelets before sphincterotomy.
Antibiotics: give prophylaxis where drainage may be incomplete or in cholangitis/obstruction.
Fasting: nil by mouth (typically ≥6h solids) to reduce aspiration risk under sedation.
🚩 Post-ERCP pancreatitis is the commonest and most feared complication. Give a prophylactic rectal NSAID (PR diclofenac or indometacin) at the time of the procedure, and consider a temporary pancreatic duct stent in high-risk cases, to reduce its incidence and severity.
🎓 MRCP is now the diagnostic test of choice for suspected biliary/pancreatic duct disease; ERCP is reserved for when therapy (stone extraction, stenting, drainage) is intended. Cannulating the ampulla of Vater requires a side-viewing duodenoscope — not the forward-viewing scope used for OGD.

Capsule (wireless video) endoscopy uses a disposable, pill-sized wireless camera that the patient swallows. As it travels passively through the GI tract by peristalsis it captures thousands of images, transmitted to a data recorder worn on a belt. Its chief value is visualising the small bowel — the segment beyond the reach of standard OGD (upper GI endoscopy) and colonoscopy — and it is then passed naturally in the stool.

1INDICATIONS — why look at the small bowel

The dominant indication is obscure GI bleeding or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia when both OGD and colonoscopy are negative, since the small bowel is otherwise a blind spot.

🩸Obscure GI bleeding
Iron-deficiency anaemia / melaena with negative OGD & colonoscopy — hunt for angiodysplasia, ulcers, tumours
🔬Crohn's disease
Assess suspected or known small-bowel Crohn's (aphthous ulcers, cobblestoning) where no stricture is present
🌾Coeliac complications
Refractory or complicated coeliac disease — ulcerative jejunitis, lymphoma surveillance
🫐Tumours & polyps
Small-bowel tumours and polyposis surveillance, e.g. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome
Anaemia + negative OGD & colonoscopy→Capsule endoscopy to image the small bowel
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Fasting (typically overnight / ~10–12 h) so the mucosa is clean and views are unobstructed.
The patient swallows the capsule with water; sensor leads and a data recorder are worn on a belt to capture the transmitted images.
The patient can usually resume light activity and eat after a couple of hours; the capsule advances passively by peristalsis — there is no sedation and no scope insertion.
Images are reviewed later by the clinician as a video; the capsule is passed naturally in the stool and discarded.
📷 Image placeholder — capsule endoscopy view of small-bowel mucosa showing an angiodysplastic lesion.
3KEY FINDINGS — what you look for
Bright red spider-like mucosal lesion→Angiodysplasia — common cause of obscure small-bowel bleeding
Aphthous ulcers, cobblestoning, skip lesions→Small-bowel Crohn's disease
Mucosal mass or polyp→Small-bowel tumour / Peutz–Jeghers polyp — refer for device-assisted enteroscopy or surgery

A crucial limitation: capsule endoscopy is purely diagnostic. It cannot take biopsies or deliver therapy (no clipping, cautery or polypectomy), and lesion localisation is only approximate — a positive finding usually needs follow-up with device-assisted (double-balloon) enteroscopy.

4COMPLICATIONS & SAFETY

The major complication is capsule retention / impaction: the capsule lodges proximal to a narrowing and can precipitate small-bowel obstruction. It is therefore contraindicated where a stricture or obstruction is known or suspected (e.g. established Crohn's stricture).

Where stricturing is a concern, a dissolvable patency capsule is swallowed first — if it passes intact, the video capsule can safely follow.
Take a careful history for dysphagia or swallowing disorders and prior obstructive symptoms before proceeding.
MRI must be avoided until the capsule is confirmed passed, as it is not MR-safe within the body.
🚩 CAPSULE RETENTION is the key risk — a retained capsule at a stricture can cause small-bowel obstruction requiring endoscopic or surgical retrieval. AVOID capsule endoscopy where stricture/obstruction is known or suspected (e.g. Crohn's stricture); use a patency capsule first. Do NOT perform MRI until the capsule is confirmed passed.
🎓 First-line small-bowel investigation for obscure GI bleeding when OGD and colonoscopy are negative is capsule endoscopy — but always exclude a stricture (patency capsule) first, because retention causing obstruction is the exam's classic complication.

Double-balloon (device-assisted) enteroscopy is a specialised long enteroscope carrying a balloon at its tip, passed through a balloon-fitted overtube. The two balloons alternately inflate and deflate to grip and “pleat” the bowel over the scope, allowing deep intubation of the small bowel far beyond the reach of standard gastroscopy or colonoscopy. Unlike capsule endoscopy, which only takes pictures, it permits BIOPSY and full THERAPEUTIC intervention under direct vision.

1INDICATIONS — diagnostic and therapeutic

It is usually a second-line, targeted tool: capsule endoscopy or cross-sectional imaging flags a lesion, and enteroscopy is then used to reach it to sample or treat.

🩸Obscure small-bowel bleeding
Argon plasma coagulation of angiodysplasia; clipping of bleeding points
🔬Polyps
Polypectomy, e.g. Peutz–Jeghers hamartomas
🎈Strictures
Balloon dilatation of Crohn’s or NSAID strictures
💊Retained capsule
Endoscopic retrieval of an impacted video capsule
🖊️Tattooing
Marking a lesion with ink before surgical resection
🧬ERCP in altered anatomy
Reaching the papilla after Roux-en-Y reconstruction
Capsule shows an actively bleeding angiodysplasia→Enteroscopy to deliver argon plasma coagulation
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — route, sedation and technique

The scope is advanced by a repeated push-and-pleat cycle: advance the scope, inflate its tip balloon to anchor, slide the overtube down and inflate its balloon, deflate the scope balloon, and withdraw both together to concertina the bowel onto the overtube — then repeat.

Antegrade (oral) — reaches the proximal and mid small bowel.
Retrograde (per anum) — passes through the colon and ileocaecal valve to reach the distal ileum.
Combined — both approaches (often with an ink tattoo at the deepest point of the first) to examine the entire small bowel.

It is performed under conscious sedation or general anaesthesia because it is lengthy and uncomfortable; fluoroscopy is sometimes used to confirm scope position.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the endoscopic view / procedure: enteroscope tip and overtube balloons pleating small-bowel loops.
3KEY FINDINGS & interventions through the scope

Under direct vision the operator inspects the mucosa and can act on findings in the same sitting.

Angiodysplasia→Argon plasma coagulation
Peutz–Jeghers polyp→Snare polypectomy
Short fibrotic stricture→Through-the-scope balloon dilatation
Suspicious mass or ulcer→Targeted biopsy ± tattoo for surgery

This is the decisive advantage over capsule endoscopy: capsule is purely diagnostic with no ability to biopsy or treat, whereas balloon enteroscopy can both sample and treat — at the cost of being invasive, time-consuming and requiring sedation or GA.

4COMPLICATIONS & pre-procedure safety

Before the procedure confirm valid consent, appropriate fasting, and review of anticoagulants and antiplatelets (correcting coagulopathy where therapy such as polypectomy is planned).

⚠️Perforation
Higher after dilatation or polypectomy
🩸Bleeding
After biopsy, polypectomy or dilatation
🔥Pancreatitis
Chiefly with the antegrade route — traction on the pancreas
💤Sedation risk
Aspiration and cardiorespiratory events from prolonged sedation/GA
🚩 Perforation and post-procedure bleeding are the major risks, but a complication near-unique to this scope is acute PANCREATITIS after the ANTEGRADE approach, caused by mechanical traction of the pleated bowel on the pancreas — suspect it if there is severe epigastric pain and a raised amylase/lipase afterwards.
🎓 Choose the route by target site: ANTEGRADE (oral) for proximal/mid small bowel, RETROGRADE (per anum) for the distal ileum. If capsule endoscopy localises the lesion, the tattoo left at the deepest antegrade point guides a subsequent retrograde study to complete whole-small-bowel examination.
